meta.titre: Consumer Arithmetic: Percentages, Profit, Discount and Interest
meta.sous_theme: Percentages, profit and loss, discount, simple and compound interest

sections.contenu_markdown: A shopkeeper at Marche Central in Douala buys a fridge from a wholesaler, adds her profit to get the marked price and then gives a discount during the end-of-year sale. A farmer deposits his harvest money in a savings account and the bank adds interest every year. Percentages are the language of money, and every Cameroonian household uses them, often without noticing. The GCE tests this topic in both papers with short Paper 1 calculations and longer Paper 2 problems, and most of the marks come from choosing the correct multiplier and the correct amount to take the percentage of.

items: A percentage is a fraction out of $100$: $5\%=\dfrac{5}{100}=0.05$.
Multiplying and dividing decimals, and converting a fraction to a decimal.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Percentage of an amount.** $r\%$ of $A$ is $\dfrac{r}{100}\times A$.

**Increase and decrease by multiplier.** To increase an amount by $r\%$, multiply it by $\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right)$. To decrease it by $r\%$, multiply by $\left(1-\dfrac{r}{100}\right)$. For example, a $30\%$ increase uses the multiplier $1.30$ and a $10\%$ decrease uses $0.90$.

**Profit and loss.** $\text{Profit}=\text{selling price}-\text{cost price}$ and $\text{Loss}=\text{cost price}-\text{selling price}$.

$$\text{Percentage profit}=\frac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost price}}\times 100\%$$

**Discount.** The discount is a percentage of the **marked price**, and the sale price is $\text{marked price}-\text{discount}$.

**Simple interest.** For principal $P$, rate $R\%$ per year and time $T$ **in years**:

$$I=\frac{PRT}{100},\qquad \text{Amount}=P+I$$

**Compound interest.** The interest is added to the principal every year, so the amount after $n$ years is

$$A=P\left(1+\frac{R}{100}\right)^{n}$$

and the compound interest is $A-P$.

**Remember.** Always say what you are taking the percentage of: profit percentage uses the cost price, a discount uses the marked price, interest uses the principal.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the new (after) value is known and you need the original value.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Divide by the multiplier. If a price after a $20\%$ discount is $8\,000$ FCFA, the multiplier is $0.80$, so the original price is $\dfrac{8\,000}{0.80}=10\,000$ FCFA. Do not add $20\%$ of $8\,000$: the $20\%$ was taken off the original, not off the new price.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you need the interest earned in each year or want to understand the formula.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Year 1: multiply by $1+\dfrac{R}{100}$. Year 2: multiply the new amount again. For $200\,000$ FCFA at $10\%$: after year 1 it is $220\,000$; after year 2 it is $242\,000$. The compound interest is $42\,000$, whereas simple interest for $2$ years is $40\,000$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A shopkeeper in Douala buys a fridge for $150\,000$ FCFA. She marks it at a price $30\%$ above the cost. In the end-of-year sale she gives a $10\%$ discount on the marked price. Calculate (a) the marked price, (b) the sale price, (c) her profit and (d) her percentage profit.

etapes.justification: A $30\%$ increase on the cost price uses the multiplier $1.30$.
A $10\%$ discount is taken off the **marked** price, so the multiplier is $0.90$.
Profit is the selling price minus the cost price.
Percentage profit is always calculated on the cost price.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The marked price is $195\,000$ FCFA, the sale price is $175\,500$ FCFA, the profit is $25\,500$ FCFA, and the percentage profit is $17\%$ (not $30\%-10\%=20\%$).

items.erreur_markdown: A price rises by $20\%$ and then falls by $20\%$, so it returns to its original value.
items.pourquoi_faux: The $20\%$ fall is calculated on the new, bigger price, so more is taken off than was added.
items.correction_markdown: $1.20\times 0.80=0.96$: the price is $4\%$ lower than at the start.

items.pourquoi_faux: Percentage profit is based on what the trader paid, the cost price, unless the question says otherwise.

items.erreur_markdown: Simple interest on $24\,000$ FCFA at $6\%$ for $6$ months: $I=\dfrac{24\,000\times 6\times 6}{100}$
items.pourquoi_faux: Time must be in years. Six months is half a year.

items.erreur_markdown: A price after a $20\%$ discount is $8\,000$ FCFA, so the original price is $8\,000+20\%$ of $8\,000=9\,600$ FCFA.
items.pourquoi_faux: The $20\%$ is a percentage of the original price. $8\,000$ is $80\%$ of the original.

items.enonce_markdown: Calculate the simple interest on $150\,000$ FCFA invested at $4\%$ per year for $3$ years. Find also the total amount at the end.
items.solution_markdown:
$I=\dfrac{PRT}{100}=\dfrac{150\,000\times 4\times 3}{100}=18\,000$ FCFA.

Amount $=150\,000+18\,000=168\,000$ FCFA.

**Answer: interest $18\,000$ FCFA; amount $168\,000$ FCFA.**

items.enonce_markdown: A pair of trousers is sold at $25\,500$ FCFA after a $15\%$ discount. Calculate (a) the original price and (b) the amount of the discount.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The sale price is $85\%$ of the original price, so the original price is $\dfrac{25\,500}{0.85}=30\,000$ FCFA.

**Answer: $30\,000$ FCFA.**

(b) Discount $=30\,000-25\,500=4\,500$ FCFA. Check: $15\%$ of $30\,000=4\,500$.

**Answer: $4\,500$ FCFA.**

items.enonce_markdown: Sandrine invests $400\,000$ FCFA at $5\%$ per year compound interest for $2$ years. Calculate (a) the amount at the end of $2$ years, (b) the compound interest, (c) how much more it is than the simple interest on the same sum over the same time.

items_markdown: $r\%$ of $A$ is $\dfrac{r}{100}\times A$; increase by $r\%$ means multiply by $1+\dfrac{r}{100}$, decrease by $r\%$ means multiply by $1-\dfrac{r}{100}$.
Percentage profit or loss is calculated on the **cost price**; a discount is calculated on the **marked price**.
Simple interest: $I=\dfrac{PRT}{100}$ with $T$ in years; compound interest: $A=P\left(1+\dfrac{R}{100}\right)^{n}$.
To find an original value, divide by the multiplier; do not add the percentage back.
Two successive percentage changes are never found by adding the percentages; multiply the multipliers.
